## The Song Before the Sword
*Mary's Magnificat and a God Who Takes Sides*

**Text:** Luke 1:46-55 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 2:1-10 · Psalm 113:7-9 · Isaiah 61:1 · Genesis 12:3

We have made this song small. We have set it to gentle music, embroidered it on banners, sung it in cathedrals with the rich in the front pews. We have done everything possible to keep it from meaning what it says.

It was sung by a pregnant teenager from a town no one respected, and it is a war song.

**A girl no court would believe**
Luke gives us the singer before he gives us the song, and the singer is the argument. She is young. She is poor. She is unmarried and showing. In her world her testimony would not have counted in a legal dispute, and yet God has entrusted the salvation of the world to her body. "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant" (Luke 1:46-48). The word for humble estate is not modesty. It is lowliness, the bottom rung, the place no one volunteers for. She is not being praised for being meek. She is naming where God looked, and God looked down. Hannah sang the same thing a thousand years earlier, barren and despised, taunted by a rival until God opened her womb, and her song became the template: "He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes" (1 Samuel 2:8). Mary is standing in a long line of women God noticed when the world did not, and she knows it. She does not sing as if something unprecedented is happening. She sings as if the God of Hannah has finally come around to her, the same God doing the same thing he has always done, choosing the overlooked one and pouring the future through her. The whole pattern of God's dealing with his people is gathered into this girl's voice, and the pattern runs in one direction. Downward, to the bottom, to the place the proud would never look.

**The verbs that scatter kings**
Then the song turns, and the verbs turn with it. "He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty" (Luke 1:51-53). Read those verbs slowly. Scattered. Brought down. Exalted. Filled. Sent away empty. This is not religious comfort layered over an unjust world. It is the overturning of it. Psalm 113 had promised it long before Mary: God "raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes" (Psalm 113:7-8). And notice the tense Mary uses. Past tense. He has done it. The thing has not happened yet by any visible measure. Rome still rules. The rich still feast. Herod still sits on his stolen throne, and the hungry are still hungry. But faith sings the victory before the battle, because the One who promised has already moved. This is the audacity of biblical hope. It does not wait for the evidence to arrive before it sings. It sings because of who made the promise, and it treats the promise as more solid than the kingdoms that look permanent. This is the same announcement Jesus will read aloud in Nazareth in chapter four, good news to the poor and liberty to the captives (Isaiah 61:1). The whole Gospel of Luke is already here, in a girl's praise, before a single sermon is preached. Everything that is coming is folded into this song. The shepherds at the bottom in chapter two. The poor called blessed on the plain in chapter six. The tax collector lifted up and the Pharisee sent away empty. The Son of Man seeking the lost all the way to a cross. Mary is not predicting some of it. She is announcing the program, and the program is reversal, the high brought low and the low brought high, and it starts in her own body, the unmarried girl God exalted to carry the King.

**The side God is on, and the trouble that is**
Here is where it stops being a pretty song and starts being a hard one. God takes sides. We do not like to say it that way, because we want a God who blesses everyone equally, who is above the fray, who does not embarrass the comfortable. But the Magnificat does embarrass the comfortable, and I am the comfortable. I have read this song from the side of the filled, not the hungry. I have more in common with the rich sent away empty than with the lowly lifted up, and I have still managed to sing it as if it were written for me. That is the problem with grace that runs downhill: those of us standing on the high ground have to come down to receive it. The mercy is real, and it is specific. "He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever" (Luke 1:54-55). This is the mercy God swore to Abraham (Genesis 12:3), and it ends at a cross, where the Son of Man came not to be filled but to be emptied, not to be exalted but brought down, so that the lowly could be lifted with him. He took the place of the rich sent away with nothing, so that the hungry could be filled. The God who takes sides took our side by losing everything.

So the question this song asks is not whether you admire Mary. It is which verb you are standing under. The proud are scattered. The humble are lifted. And the only way down to the second is to stop defending the first.

God has chosen the lowly.

## Glory on the Night Shift
*The Birth at the Bottom and the Witnesses Who Did Not Count*

**Text:** Luke 2:1-20 · **Supporting:** Micah 5:2 · Isaiah 9:6 · 1 Corinthians 1:27-28 · Philippians 2:7

Luke tells you exactly when it happened, and then he refuses to take you where you would expect to go.

He names the emperor. He names the governor. And then he walks past the palace without a glance.

**Dated by Caesar, ignored by Luke**
"In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria" (Luke 2:1-2). Luke is a careful historian, and he plants the birth in real time, under a real census, by a real decree from the most powerful man alive. Augustus snaps his fingers and the whole Mediterranean world moves, a carpenter and his pregnant wife among them, dragged eighty miles to Bethlehem because an emperor wants a tax roll. The census is a display of power. Every name written down is a name Rome owns, a body Rome can count and tax and conscript. And here is what Luke does with all that imperial machinery: he uses it to get Mary to Bethlehem, where the prophet Micah said the ruler of Israel would be born, "whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days" (Micah 5:2). Caesar thinks he is collecting taxes. He is fulfilling a prophecy he never read. The real King is being born under the nose of the man who thinks he is king, and the man never finds out. That is the quiet joke running underneath the whole scene. The most powerful man in the world issues a decree, and the decree serves a purpose he could not see and would have crushed if he had. Empires think they move history. They do not even know what is happening in the towns they tax. The decade's most important event takes place in a stable on the edge of the empire, and the empire records only that a few more names were added to the roll.

**No room, and a feeding trough**
Then comes the line we have decorated until it stopped hurting. "And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn" (Luke 2:7). A manger is a feeding trough. Strip the figurines off it. The Savior of the world enters the world among the animals because there was no room for him in the place where people belonged. Isaiah called him "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6), and the Prince of Peace is laid in the box where the livestock eat. This is not an accident of crowded lodging. This is the shape of the whole thing. Paul will say it plainly: he "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7). The descent that ends at the cross begins at the trough. God did not arrive at the top and reach down. He started at the bottom and stayed there. We have a religious instinct that runs the opposite way, always upward, always toward the impressive, always assuming that the closer something is to power the closer it must be to God. The manger kills that instinct. The God of Israel chose the feeding trough on purpose, and he chose it first, before the cross, so that no one could ever mistake where he was willing to be found.

**The announcement to the men who did not count**
Now watch where the announcement goes, because this is the sermon. There are kings within reach. There are priests in Jerusalem. There are respectable, religious, credentialed men all over that country. And the angel goes to none of them. "And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night" (Luke 2:8). Shepherds worked the night shift. They were poor, they were dirty, and their testimony was considered so unreliable that it was not admitted in court. These are men whose word did not count. And to these men, on this shift, "the glory of the Lord shone around them" (Luke 2:9). The glory that filled the temple, that Moses could not look at directly, comes down on the people Rome counted only for taxation, the people no judge would believe. God chose the witnesses no one would trust to testify to the event no one would expect.

And I have to sit inside that, because I would not have chosen them. I would have sent the news to the people who matter, to the platform with the biggest reach, to the room where decisions are made. We always do. The church does it constantly, courting the influential and stepping over the night shift, building strategies around the people whose word counts and quietly forgetting the people whose word does not. We did the second and called it the first. But the God who announced his Son to shepherds is still announcing him to the overlooked, and the danger is not that we are too lowly to hear it. The danger is that we are too important to be standing in the field. Paul saw it: God "chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are" (1 Corinthians 1:28). The glory came to the men who did not count, because the Son of Man came to seek the ones the world had stopped counting, and one day he would be counted among them, numbered with the transgressors, no room for him even on a cross meant for someone else.

The shepherds went back to the night shift. But they went back "glorifying and praising God" (Luke 2:20), still poor, still on the margin, carrying the one piece of news that the emperor would have killed to suppress and never even heard.

Glory came to the night shift.

## The Sermon That Almost Got Him Killed
*The Nazareth Manifesto and the Grace the Hometown Could Not Forgive*

**Text:** Luke 4:16-30 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 61:1-2 · 1 Kings 17:8-16 · 2 Kings 5:1-14 · Jonah 4:1-2

The first sermon Jesus preaches in his hometown ends with the congregation trying to throw him off a cliff.

We should want to know what he said. It was one sentence past the line they could bear.

**The text he chose, and the line he stopped on**
He goes home to Nazareth, to the synagogue where he was raised, and they hand him the scroll of Isaiah. He finds the place and reads: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor" (Luke 4:18-19). Then he rolls up the scroll, sits down, and says, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21). That is the claim. Not someday. Not in heaven. Today, in this room, in me. And notice where he stopped reading. The passage in Isaiah goes on to "the day of vengeance of our God" (Isaiah 61:2). Jesus reads the favor and stops before the vengeance. He closes the scroll on the mercy. That editorial cut is not careless; it is the announcement of what kind of Messiah he intends to be. They wanted the vengeance. They wanted the day the Lord would burn the Gentiles and lift up Israel, and Jesus reads right up to the edge of that line and folds the scroll. He came preaching favor first. The hometown crowd hears the good news, and at first they are delighted, marveling at the gracious words from Joseph's boy. They are ready to claim him. He is theirs. The local carpenter's son made good, the hometown hero, and they want to ride his rising the way every small town wants to claim the famous son who left and came back.

**The two stories that turned the room**
Then he tells them two stories, and the room turns. He reminds them that in the days of Elijah there were many widows in Israel during the famine, "and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow" (Luke 4:25-26). A foreigner. A pagan. Fed by God while Israel's own widows went hungry (1 Kings 17:8-16). Then the second: there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha, "and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian" (Luke 4:27). An enemy general. The commander of the army that raided Israel, healed in the Jordan while Israel's lepers stayed sick (2 Kings 5:1-14). Jesus is telling his own town that the favor of the Lord he just announced is real, and it reaches past Nazareth to the outsider, to the foreigner, to the enemy. The grace he came to bring does not stop at the border of the people who feel entitled to it. And that is the line they cannot forgive. "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff" (Luke 4:28-29). They loved the good news right up until they learned it was not exclusively theirs. Notice how fast the turn is. One minute they are speaking well of him, marveling, proud of the local boy. The next minute they have him by the brow of a cliff. Nothing changed except that he told them God's mercy had a history of leaping over the chosen and landing on the outsider. The same fact that thrilled them when they thought it was for them enraged them the moment they learned it was for everyone. That is the speed at which religious pride turns to violence, and it turns on a single word.

**The grace that enrages the insider**
Here is the thing I have to own, because I am the insider in this story. I am the hometown. It is easy to read this and feel superior to Nazareth, to shake my head at people so small they would kill a man over a sermon. But the wrath in that synagogue is not the wrath of obviously wicked people. It is the wrath of religious people who assumed grace ran on their terms and discovered it did not. And I have felt that exact wrath. I have been glad for the gospel right up until it included someone I had written off, the person of the wrong politics, the wrong past, the wrong tribe, and then something in me wanted to drive it off a cliff. Grace for me is comfort. Grace for the outsider is an offense, and the offense is the test. Jonah had the same sickness centuries before, angry that God would spare Nineveh, so angry he wanted to die, because he knew God was "a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love" (Jonah 4:2), and he could not stand it being aimed at the enemy. The favor of the Lord enrages the insider precisely because it is favor, unearned, undeserved, and therefore not ours to ration.

And notice how the scene ends. "But passing through their midst, he went away" (Luke 4:30). The grace they tried to kill simply walks through the mob. It is not stopped by their wrath, and it is not contained by their borders. The same Jesus who reached past Nazareth to a Syrian and a Sidonian widow is the Son of Man who came to seek the lost wherever they were, including the lost insider standing at the edge of the cliff with murder in his heart, still loved, still being preached to, still given one more sentence of good news he did not want to hear.

Grace for outsiders enrages the insiders.

## The Catch That Made Him Afraid
*Peter on His Knees in a Sinking Boat*

**Text:** Luke 5:1-11 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 6:1-8 · Job 42:5-6 · Psalm 51:5 · 1 Timothy 1:15

The nets are full and the boats are sinking and the catch is everything Peter has worked his whole life to bring in.

And Peter's response is to beg the man who gave it to him to go away.

**The all-night failure and the daylight word**
Peter is a professional. He has fished these waters his whole life, and he knows what he is doing, and he has done it all night and caught nothing. "Master, we toiled all night and took nothing" (Luke 5:5). That is the voice of a man who is tired, who knows his trade, and who has nothing to show for it. Then a carpenter from Nazareth, of all people, tells the fisherman where to fish. "But at your word I will let down the nets" (Luke 5:5). And the catch comes in so heavy the nets begin to break, so heavy they signal the other boat, so heavy both boats begin to sink under the weight of it (Luke 5:6-7). This is abundance past anything Peter's skill could produce, arriving precisely where his skill had failed, on the word of a man who should know nothing about fishing. The miracle is not just a full net. It is a full net at the exact point of Peter's expertise and his emptiness, so he cannot mistake it for luck. God often works this way, meeting a man precisely where he is most confident and most defeated at the same time, the place he knows best and the place he has just failed, so that the gift cannot be filed away as coincidence or skill. Peter could explain a small catch. He cannot explain this. The nets do not break for an ordinary haul, and two boats do not sink under good fortune. Something is in his boat that does not belong to his world, and the abundance is the evidence.

**Dread, not delight**
Now watch Peter's reaction, because it is not what you would expect. He does not celebrate. He does not count the money. "When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus's knees, saying, Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord" (Luke 5:8). The full boat does not make Peter happy. It makes him afraid. Because in that catch he has seen something he cannot explain, a power that does not belong to a carpenter, and nearness to that kind of holiness does not feel like comfort. It feels like exposure. This is what always happens when a sinner gets close to the real God. Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple and did not say how wonderful. He said, "Woe is me, for I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips" (Isaiah 6:5). Job had heard about God his whole life, and when he finally saw him he said, "Now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes" (Job 42:5-6). Holiness does not flatter. It reveals. And Peter, standing in his own sinking boat, suddenly cannot bear the proximity, because the light has fallen on what he is. "Depart from me." Leave. I am not safe to be near. This is the reaction of a man who has actually met God, and it is the opposite of the casual familiarity we often bring to him. We tend to assume that getting closer to God is comfortable, warm, reassuring. But the people in Scripture who actually drew near to his holiness fell down, covered their faces, begged for distance. Peter is not being falsely modest. He has seen something true about the gap between what he is and who is standing in his boat, and the honest response to that gap is dread.

**He does not leave**
And here is the gospel in a single refusal. Jesus does not leave. The sinner asks him to go, names his own unworthiness, makes the honest plea of a man who knows he does not belong in that company, and Jesus stays. "Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men" (Luke 5:10). He does not say Peter is wrong about himself. Peter is not wrong. He is a sinful man, and so am I, and the closer either of us gets to Christ the more obvious it becomes. But the confession of sin is not the thing that drives Jesus away. It is the thing he calls. He calls the man who flinched. He calls the one who fell down and asked him to leave. The whole pattern of the gospel is here: not that we draw near because we are clean, but that he draws near while we are not, and refuses to go when we beg him to. Paul, who knew exactly what he had been, said it for all of us: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). The foremost. The one most aware he should be told to depart. That is who gets the call.

And I know which man I am in this boat. I am not the one standing confident before the holiness of God. I am the one on my knees in the bottom of the boat, hoping he will not look too closely, half-wanting him to leave because being seen is unbearable. The temptation is to think the goal of the Christian life is to become impressive enough that Jesus would want to stay. It is the opposite. The whole point is that he stays with the man who knows he is sinful, who has nothing to offer but a confession, who is exposed by the very glory he is kneeling in. The Son of Man came to seek and save exactly that man. Not the fisherman who had a good night. The one who toiled all night and took nothing, and then could not stop trembling when he saw who was in his boat.

"And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him" (Luke 5:11). They left the largest catch of their lives lying on the shore. Because once you have been called by the one you begged to leave, the nets do not matter anymore.

He calls the ones who flinch.

## Level Ground
*Blessings, Woes, and the Love That Only the Father Can Supply*

**Text:** Luke 6:20-36 · **Supporting:** Matthew 5:43-45 · Romans 5:8 · Leviticus 19:18 · Psalm 103:8-10

Jesus comes down the mountain and does not go back up to preach. He stands on level ground, in the crowd, eye to eye with the poor.

And from there he tears up the scoreboard everyone in that field had spent their lives keeping.

**Down on the plain**
Luke is careful about the geography, because the geography is the message. "And he came down with them and stood on a level place" (Luke 6:17). Not above the crowd on a hillside. With them, on flat ground, at their level. And then he lifts up his eyes on his disciples and starts naming the people the world had written off. "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. Blessed are you when people hate you" (Luke 6:20-22). Look at who he is calling blessed. The poor. The hungry. The weeping. The hated. These are not spiritual categories he is softening into metaphor. These are the people at the bottom of every social ledger, and he stands on their level and tells them the kingdom is theirs. The scoreboard of the world reads them as losers. Jesus reads the scoreboard upside down.

**The woes nobody quotes**
And then he says the part we leave out of the wall art. "But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Woe to you when all people speak well of you" (Luke 6:24-26). The rich. The full. The laughing. The well-regarded. The exact people the world envies, the people whose lives look like proof of God's favor, and Jesus pronounces woe over them. Not because money is a sin or laughter is a crime, but because comfort is the most reliable anesthetic against need, and the kingdom comes to the needy. The danger of being full is that you stop being hungry for God. The danger of everyone speaking well of you is that you have arranged your life to be approved by the very world the kingdom is overturning. And I have to be honest about which column I am in. By the measures of human history I am rich, I am full, I am generally well-regarded, and I have read these woes as if they applied to billionaires and not to me. They apply to me. The woe is not aimed at someone richer than me. It is aimed at the consolation I have already received and called blessing.

**The standard no reciprocity can reach**
Then, having inverted the scoreboard, he raises the standard past anything human exchange can reach. "But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you" (Luke 6:27-28). The old law said love your neighbor (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus extends it to the one place no instinct will follow: the enemy. And he closes the door on every transaction we might hide behind. "If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them" (Luke 6:32). Anyone can run that math. Love returned for love is just accounting. Then the command that has no floor under it: "Lend, expecting nothing in return" (Luke 6:35). No return. No hold over them. No quiet ledger of what they owe you now. This is a love with the profit motive cut out, and that is exactly why it cannot come from us. It is not in our nature. Reciprocity is in our nature. This is not.

So where does it come from. Jesus tells us, and it is the hinge of the whole sermon. "Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36). The pattern is the Father. We are to love our enemies because that is precisely what God did. "While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). We were the enemy. Not the difficult neighbor, not the rival, the enemy, opposed to him, and God did not wait for us to come around. "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). The Father does not treat us as our sins deserve (Psalm 103:10). He sends rain on the just and the unjust, kindness on the ungrateful and the evil (Luke 6:35). The love Jesus commands on the plain is impossible until you have first received it from the cross, where the enemy was loved at infinite cost, and then it is not a strain but an overflow. You cannot lend expecting nothing until you have first been forgiven a debt you could never repay. The order is everything here, and we keep reversing it. We hear love your enemies as a command to grit our teeth and try harder, and we fail, because the human heart does not generate this kind of love on demand. It receives it first. The mercy comes down from the Father, lands on the man who knows he was the enemy, and only then begins to flow outward toward the enemy still standing in front of him. Strain produces nothing but resentment. Mercy received produces mercy given.

The Son of Man came down to level ground to seek the poor and the hated, and he loved his enemies all the way to a cross, praying forgiveness over the men driving the nails. He did not command a love he was unwilling to die demonstrating. The standard is impossible. He met it on our behalf, and now he gives us his own Spirit to begin, imperfectly, to live it.

Love the ones who hate you.

## The Woman Who Wept on His Feet
*Forgiven Much, Loving Much, at a Respectable Man's Table*

**Text:** Luke 7:36-50 · **Supporting:** Psalm 51:17 · Romans 5:20 · 1 John 4:19 · Luke 18:9-14

A respectable man invites Jesus to dinner, and a woman the whole town knows as a sinner crashes it.

By the end of the night, only one of them goes home forgiven, and it is not the host.

**The crash and the calculation**
The scene is set with two people in the same room having opposite reactions to the same Jesus. There is Simon the Pharisee, who has done everything correctly, opened his home, invited the teacher, observed the forms. And there is a woman "who was a sinner" (Luke 7:37), her reputation known to everyone, who walks into a dinner where she was not invited and does something undignified and unrepeatable. "And standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment" (Luke 7:38). She is weeping so hard her tears fall on his feet. She lets down her hair in public, which a respectable woman did not do, and uses it as a towel. She is past caring how this looks. Meanwhile the host watches, and says nothing aloud, but Luke lets us hear his thoughts. "If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner" (Luke 7:39). Simon has just decided Jesus is no prophet. The irony is that Jesus is at that moment reading Simon's mind.

**The parable that turns on the host**
So Jesus tells a story, a small one, about money. A moneylender had two debtors, one who owed five hundred denarii and one who owed fifty, "and when they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?" (Luke 7:42). Simon answers correctly, a little warily, "The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt" (Luke 7:43). And then Jesus turns the whole parable around and aims it at the host. He goes through the courtesies Simon skipped: no water for his feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for his head. And then, point by point, the woman. "She has wet my feet with her tears. She has not ceased to kiss my feet. She anointed my feet with ointment" (Luke 7:44-46). And then the verdict that has been misread for centuries. "Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little" (Luke 7:47). Read it carefully. Her love is not the cause of her forgiveness. Her love is the evidence of it. The debtor does not earn the cancellation by being grateful; he is grateful because the debt was cancelled. Her tears are not a payment. They are a response. She has already been forgiven, somewhere, somehow, in a previous encounter we are not shown, and the weeping is what forgiveness looks like when it lands on a soul that knows exactly how much it owed.

**The danger of owing little**
Here is the part that should worry the respectable, and I am the respectable. "He who is forgiven little, loves little." Notice Jesus does not say Simon was forgiven nothing. He says little, and that is the trap. Simon does not love much because Simon does not think he owes much. He has kept the rules. He has stayed clean. He sits at his own table dry-eyed while a known sinner weeps on the floor, and he pities her, and he congratulates himself on the distance between them, and that distance is the whole problem. The one who thinks his debt is small will love in proportion to his self-assessment, which is to say barely at all. And I have spent more of my life at Simon's end of the table than I want to admit. I have been the man who kept the forms, who did the courtesies, who looked at the obvious sinner and felt a quiet, fatal sense of being a few rungs higher. That sense is the thing that keeps me dry-eyed. The tragedy of the Pharisee is not that he sinned too much. It is that he never grasped how much he was forgiven, and so he never learned to love. The tax collector in the later parable beat his breast and would not lift his eyes and went home justified, while the Pharisee thanking God he was not like other men went home with nothing (Luke 18:9-14). Same sickness. Same table.

The woman understood something Simon never did. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17). She came broken, and she left whole. "Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more" (Romans 5:20), and she was living proof, the one whose enormous debt made the cancellation enormous, whose love poured out in exact measure to the mercy poured in. "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). She loved much because she had been loved first, much, by the one who would soon let his own feet be pierced to pay the debt she could not. And Jesus sends her out not with a lecture but with a gift. "Your faith has saved you; go in peace" (Luke 7:50). She walks out forgiven. The host stays at his clean, correct, dry-eyed table, and we are not told he ever wept. That is the quiet horror of the ending. The sinner leaves saved and the saint stays stuck, and the difference between them was never the size of the sin. It was the size of the debt each one knew he owed. The woman knew exactly what she had been forgiven, and it broke her open into love. Simon assumed he owed almost nothing, and so he received almost nothing, and felt no need to. The most dangerous place to stand before God is not the place of obvious sin. It is the place of quiet respectability, where you have kept enough rules to convince yourself the cancellation was small.

Forgiven much, she loved much.

## A Death With No Plan B
*Take Up the Cross Daily, and the Three Who Almost Followed*

**Text:** Luke 9:23-27, 57-62 · **Supporting:** Galatians 2:20 · Philippians 3:8 · Mark 10:21-22 · 1 Kings 19:19-21

We have a way of presenting Jesus that he never authorized. We make him easy to follow.

Then you read the words he actually used, and they are the words of a man asking for your life.

**The terms, stated plainly**
There is no fine print here, no soft sell, no minimum payment. "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me" (Luke 9:23). Three things, and each one cuts. Deny himself, which means dethrone the self that runs your life. Take up his cross, which to that crowd meant one thing only, the instrument the Romans used to execute the condemned, the beam you carried to your own death. And then the word Luke alone adds, daily. Not a single dramatic decision but a death repeated every morning. And Jesus explains the terrible arithmetic of it. "For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it" (Luke 9:24). The instinct that runs all of us, the instinct to save ourselves, to protect the life we have built, is precisely the instinct that destroys us. The only way to keep your life is to hand it over. This is not a motivational paradox. It is a cross, and crosses are not metaphors to the people who have to carry them.

**The three at the roadside**
Luke then shows us what those terms look like when real people meet them, and Jesus does not soften the price for any of them. The first volunteers freely: "I will follow you wherever you go" (Luke 9:57). And Jesus does not thank him. He warns him. "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head" (Luke 9:58). Count the cost. Following me means homelessness, means insecurity, means a Master poorer than the animals. The second is invited by Jesus, and asks one reasonable thing: "Let me first go and bury my father" (Luke 9:59). This is not laziness. This is a sacred duty, the burial of a parent, the most basic obligation a son had. And Jesus says the hardest thing in the passage: "Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:60). Even this cannot come first. The third asks only to say goodbye to his family, the very thing Elisha was permitted to do when Elijah called him from the plow (1 Kings 19:19-21). And Jesus, who let Elisha have his farewell, will not let this man have his: "No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:62). Three would-be followers, three good reasons, three refusals to lower the bar. Luke will not let discipleship be a sentiment. It is a death, and a death has no plan B.

**The cost we keep negotiating**
Now I have to be honest about how I read these three, because I am all three of them. I am the man who says I will follow anywhere and then flinches when anywhere turns out to mean discomfort. I am the man with a legitimate obligation I keep placing ahead of the call, and the obligation is always reasonable, that is what makes it dangerous. I am the man with his hand on the plow looking back at the life he left, mourning the thing he chose to give up. We have built an entire Christianity around negotiating these terms down, around finding the version of following Jesus that costs roughly what we were already willing to pay. The rich young ruler did it; he wanted eternal life on terms that let him keep his wealth, and when Jesus named the price "he became very sad, for he was extremely rich" (Mark 10:22), and walked away from the only one who could save him because the cost was too high. We have all walked a few steps down that road. We want the resurrection without the cross, the saving of our life without the losing of it, and Jesus keeps telling us it does not come in that order.

But hear the other half, because the demand is not cruelty. The one who calls you to die is the one who died for you first. He did not ask the crowd to carry a cross he was unwilling to carry. He set his face to Jerusalem in this very chapter, walking toward his own execution, taking up the literal cross so that ours could be, in the end, a death that leads to life. "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). That is not a loss. That is the trade Paul called everything else garbage by comparison: "I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). The Son of Man with nowhere to lay his head came to seek the lost, and what he offers is worth more than the life he asks you to lay down to get it. He is not taking your life from you. He is taking it so he can give it back to you alive.

The terms have not changed. They will never change. He is still standing at the roadside, still refusing to make it easy, still worth it. And the daily part is the mercy hidden inside the demand. He did not say take up your cross once, in a single heroic moment, and then coast. He said daily, because he knows we will fail at it every morning and need to come back to it every morning. The cross is not a one-time entrance fee. It is the shape of a life, picked up again at dawn, dropped by noon, picked up again, the slow daily death of a self that does not want to die and a Savior who keeps calling it down off the throne. He does not ask for a single grand sacrifice you could be proud of. He asks for the unglamorous, repeated surrender of an ordinary Tuesday.

Follow him, or do not.

## The Heretic Who Stopped
*The Good Samaritan and the Neighbor the Lawyer Despised*

**Text:** Luke 10:25-37 · **Supporting:** Micah 6:8 · James 2:15-16 · Leviticus 19:18 · 1 John 3:17-18

A lawyer asks Jesus a question designed to get himself off the hook, and Jesus tells a story that puts the hook through the man's own conscience.

The hero turns out to be the one person in the room the lawyer could not stand.

**The question behind the question**
The lawyer's first question is large: "Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" (Luke 10:25). Jesus turns it back, and the lawyer answers well, quoting the law: love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself (Luke 10:27, Leviticus 19:18). Correct. Do this and live. But then Luke tells us the man's motive, and it changes everything. "But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, And who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29). He is not asking out of curiosity. He is asking to draw a line. If he can define neighbor narrowly enough, he can prove he has already cleared the bar. The whole question is an attempt to shrink the command down to a size he has already satisfied. We do this constantly. We ask who exactly we are obligated to love so we can confirm it does not include the people we were never going to love anyway.

**The road, and the men who passed**
So Jesus tells a story. A man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, a notoriously dangerous road, is stripped, beaten, and left half dead. Then come the two men the lawyer would most expect to be the heroes. "Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side" (Luke 10:31-32). A priest and a Levite. The religious professionals. The people whose entire vocation was the service of God. And both of them see the bleeding man and cross to the far side of the road. They may have had reasons, ritual purity, fear of a trap, the press of duties elsewhere. The reasons do not matter to the man in the ditch. They saw, and they passed. And then the figure no one in the lawyer's world would cast as the hero. "But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion" (Luke 10:33). A Samaritan. To this lawyer, a half-breed, a heretic, a man whose worship was wrong and whose blood was impure, the despised people. That is who stops.

And watch how thoroughly he stops. He binds the wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He sets the man on his own animal and walks. He brings him to an inn and cares for him through the night. The next day he pays the innkeeper two denarii, two days' wages, and makes an open-ended promise: "Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back" (Luke 10:35). This is not a gesture. This is cost, time, money, risk, and a return trip pledged. The heretic does what the priest would not.

**The question Jesus refuses to answer**
Then Jesus does something brilliant. The lawyer asked, who is my neighbor, meaning whom am I obligated to love. Jesus refuses to answer that question. Instead he asks a different one. "Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?" (Luke 10:36). Do you see the reversal. The lawyer wanted to identify the category of person he was required to love so he could stay inside his comfort. Jesus will not let him define the neighbor at all. He makes him define the love. The question is not who qualifies as my neighbor. The question is whether I will become one to whoever is bleeding in front of me. And the lawyer cannot even say the word Samaritan. He answers, "The one who showed him mercy" (Luke 10:37). Mercy, not bloodline. Mercy, not correct theology. Mercy is the proof of love for God, and the Lord had said it through Micah long before: he requires us "to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8).

And I am not the Samaritan in this story. I would like to be, but honesty puts me on the far side of the road with the priest. I have seen the bleeding man, the need right in front of me, and found a reason, a good reason, a busy and important reason, to cross to the other side. The most dangerous distance in this parable is the width of a road, and I have walked it. James names exactly this self-deception: if you see a brother in need and say "go in peace, be warmed and filled, without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?" (James 2:16). Love that crosses the road is no love at all. "Let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth" (1 John 3:18).

There is one more turn. The lawyer asked how to inherit eternal life by what he could do. The story shows him a standard he cannot meet, a mercy more total than his, and points past itself to the one who finally fulfilled it. Because there was a Man who came down our dangerous road, who saw us beaten and stripped and half dead, who did not pass by on the other side, who paid not two denarii but his own blood, and who has promised to come back. The Son of Man came to seek the one in the ditch. We are not first the Samaritan. We are first the man he rescued. And only because he became our neighbor at the cost of his life can we now go and become one to somebody else.

Go and do likewise. Which means stop.

The despised one was the neighbor.

## Knock Like You Mean It
*The Shameless Friend at Midnight and the Father Who Delights to Give*

**Text:** Luke 11:1-13 · **Supporting:** Matthew 7:11 · Psalm 145:18-19 · Isaiah 30:18 · Romans 8:15-16

The disciples watch Jesus pray and ask him to teach them, and the prayer he gives them is shockingly short.

Then he spends the rest of the lesson convincing them the Father is not the obstacle they imagine.

**The short prayer**
First, notice how little he gives them. We expect the master of prayer to hand over a long and elaborate liturgy. Instead, a few clauses. "Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation" (Luke 11:2-4). That is nearly the whole thing. It begins with God, not with us, his name hallowed, his kingdom coming, before a single request for ourselves. Then it turns to need, and the needs are humble and daily: bread for today, not security for a decade. Forgiveness, tied to our forgiving. Rescue from the testing we cannot bear. There is no flattery in it, no long preamble to soften God up, no working him into a generous mood. It assumes a Father who is already disposed to give. The brevity is the theology. You do not have to talk God into anything.

**The man at the door**
But Jesus knows our hearts do not believe that, so he tells a story about persistence. A man has an unexpected guest at midnight and no bread to set before him, so he goes to a friend's house and pounds on the door. The friend, already in bed with the children, calls out the most natural thing in the world: "Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything" (Luke 11:7). Leave me alone. It is the middle of the night. And here is the engine of the parable. "I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs" (Luke 11:8). That word, impudence, is shamelessness, the refusal to be embarrassed into going home. The man keeps knocking. He will not be put off by the closed door, the late hour, the irritated voice. And he gets the bread. Then the famous lines: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you" (Luke 11:9). Not ask once and shrug. Ask, seek, knock, the verbs of a man who will not leave the door.

**The argument from lesser to greater**
Now watch the logic, because this is where the whole lesson lands and where Jesus dismantles the lie we carry about God. The parable is not saying God is the reluctant sleeper who has to be badgered. It is the opposite. It argues from lesser to greater. "What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?" (Luke 11:11-12). No father does that. Then the turn: "If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him" (Luke 11:13). How much more. If a sleepy, annoyed neighbor will eventually get up, if a flawed and even evil human father still hands his child bread and not a stone, then how much more the Father whose goodness has no flaw in it. The point of the midnight friend is not that God is reluctant like the sleeper. It is that even a reluctant sleeper gives in, so how much more the Father who is not reluctant at all. "The Lord is near to all who call on him, to all who call on him in truth" (Psalm 145:18).

And I confess I pray most days as if the opposite were true. I pray like a man trying to wear down a God who would rather not be bothered, knocking timidly, half-expecting the irritated voice through the door, ready to apologize for the intrusion. The persistence Jesus commands is not for grinding down a reluctant God. It is the persistence of a child who is so sure of the Father's goodness that he will not stop asking, because he knows the door is going to open. We have it backward. We think the long, repeated knocking is to overcome God's reluctance, when in fact the reluctance is all in us, the unbelief that he is good, the suspicion that he is the sleeper and not the Father. Isaiah saw the truth of him: "The Lord waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you" (Isaiah 30:18). He waits to be gracious. The delay is never his unwillingness.

And notice the gift at the end. Not just bread, not just the answer to the immediate request, but the Holy Spirit, God giving us himself. The Son of Man who came to seek the lost teaches the lost to call God Father, and then gives the Spirit who cries within us, "Abba, Father" (Romans 8:15-16), so that the very prayer begins not with our reaching up but with his Spirit reaching down. We do not pray to a stranger behind a locked door. We pray to a Father who has already adopted us, who delights to give, whose hand is open before we ever knock.

So knock. Keep knocking. Not because the door is hard to open, but because the Father on the other side is better than your fear of him. And when the answer is slow, do not read the delay as reluctance. Read it the way the parable teaches, as the silence of a Father who is already up, already moving, already glad to give, whose timing is part of the gift and not the withholding of it. The man at midnight kept knocking and got the bread. He did not get it because he wore his friend down into generosity. He got it because the asking is exactly what a child does who knows the house belongs to a good Father.

Ask the Father who delights to give.

## The Father Who Runs
*Two Lost Sons and a Love That Goes Out to Both*

**Text:** Luke 15:11-32 · **Supporting:** Romans 5:8 · Ephesians 2:8-9 · Jonah 4:1-3 · Isaiah 64:6

Jesus tells this story to silence a complaint, and we have spent two thousand years missing which son the complaint belonged to.

There are two lost sons in this house. Only one of them ever comes home.

**The complaint that started it**
Do not lose why Jesus tells this. "Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, This man receives sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:1-2). The respectable are offended that Jesus keeps company with the disreputable. So Jesus tells three parables about lost things found, and the third has a second half aimed straight at the grumblers. Keep that frame the whole way through, because the parable is not finally about the wild younger son at all. It is about the people standing there complaining that grace is being wasted on the wrong people.

**The son who wished his father dead**
The younger son asks for his inheritance, and we have softened what that means. "Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me" (Luke 15:12). An inheritance comes when a father dies. The son is saying he wishes his father were already dead; he wants the money now and the man gone. It is a death wish dressed as a financial request. He takes it, goes to a far country, and squanders it, and ends up so low he is feeding pigs and envying their food, a Jewish boy at the absolute bottom (Luke 15:13-16). Then he "came to himself" and rehearses a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants" (Luke 15:18-19). He is coming home to negotiate, to earn his way back as a hired hand, because he cannot imagine being received as a son.

And then the picture that breaks the story open. "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The father had been watching the road. He sees him far off, which means he had never stopped looking. And he runs. A dignified man in that culture did not run; it meant gathering up his robes and exposing his legs, a humiliation. The father humiliates himself to reach his son faster. The boy starts his rehearsed speech, gets through the part about being unworthy, and never reaches the part about being a hired servant, because the father cuts him off and calls for the robe, the ring, the feast (Luke 15:22-24). The son came to earn his way back to a lower status. The father gives him sonship before he can finish apologizing. "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). While we were still a long way off.

**The son who stayed and was just as lost**
Now Jesus turns the camera, because this is the half for the grumblers. The elder son comes in from the field, hears the music, learns his brother is home and a feast is on, "and he was angry and refused to go in" (Luke 15:28). And listen to his complaint, because it is the complaint of every respectable, rule-keeping person who has ever resented grace. "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat" (Luke 15:29). Served. Like a slave, not a son. He has lived in his father's house for years and never understood that he was a son, never enjoyed it, kept the rules with a grinding resentment, waiting for the wages he felt he had earned. He is just as lost as his brother, but lost in the field instead of the far country, lost in his own self-righteousness instead of his sin. And his sin is uglier in one way, because the younger son knew he was lost and the elder does not. He cannot even call the prodigal his brother; he says "this son of yours" (Luke 15:30).

And here the father does the thing we always forget. He goes out a second time. "His father came out and entreated him" (Luke 15:28). He ran to the younger son in the road, and he goes out and pleads with the elder son in the yard. Both sons are outside the feast. Both have to be gone out to. The father pursues them both, the one lost in rebellion and the one lost in resentment, and the story ends without telling us whether the elder son goes in, because the grumbling Pharisees standing in front of Jesus are the elder son, and the ending is left open so they can write it themselves.

I know which son I am, and it is not the one I would prefer. I am rarely the prodigal in the far country. I am the elder brother in the field, who has kept the rules and is quietly furious that grace is free, who serves like a hired hand and calls it faithfulness, who looks at the obvious sinner being welcomed and feels not joy but the cold complaint that I have earned more than this. That is the lostness that is hardest to see, because it looks like obedience. My righteousness is the problem, not the solution; even my best is "a polluted garment" (Isaiah 64:6), and the elder son's years of service were never the price of his father's love, which was free the whole time. Salvation "is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9), and the elder son's whole life was a boast he was waiting to cash in. Jonah sat outside Nineveh furious that God forgave the people he hated (Jonah 4:1-3), and the elder son sits outside the feast furious for the same reason. The far country is not the only place you can be lost. You can be lost in your father's own field.

But the gospel is in the father's feet, both times. He runs to the rebel and he goes out to the resenter, and behind that running father is the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost, every kind of lost, who left the safety of heaven and humiliated himself, robe gathered up, all the way to a cross, to bring both sons home. The feast is ready. The only question the story leaves open is whether the elder son will let himself need it.

The Father runs toward the lost.

## The Name He Knew Too Late
*The Rich Man, the Beggar at the Gate, and the Sin of Stepping Over*

**Text:** Luke 16:19-31 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 15:7-8 · James 2:15-16 · Amos 6:4-6 · 1 John 3:17

There are two men in this story, and only one of them has a name.

That is the first thing wrong, and the whole parable is built on it.

**The gate between them**
Jesus draws the picture with brutal economy. "There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day" (Luke 16:19). Purple was the color of royalty, the most expensive dye in the world, and he wore it ordinarily, every day, the way some people wear comfort like a uniform. And "at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores" (Luke 16:20-21). At his gate. Not across the city, not in some distant country whose suffering is easy to abstract. At the gate the rich man walked through every single day. The beggar is named, Lazarus, which means God is my help, and the rich man is not named at all, and that reversal is deliberate. In the eyes of the world the rich man is somebody and the beggar is nobody. Jesus knows the beggar's name and never bothers to record the rich man's.

**The reversal beyond appeal**
Then both men die, and the positions flip completely and permanently. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man is buried, and finds himself in torment (Luke 16:22-23). And here is the detail that indicts him. From his torment, "he called out, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue" (Luke 16:24). He knows the beggar's name. He knew it all along. Lazarus was not an anonymous lump at the gate; the rich man knew exactly who he was and stepped over him anyway, day after day, and now in torment the name comes easily to his lips, as an errand boy he expects can still be sent to serve him. Even now he assumes Lazarus exists to fetch him water. The contempt survives death. And Abraham tells him the gulf is fixed, that none can cross it now (Luke 16:25-26). The reversal is beyond appeal. The time for the gate to matter was during life, and that time is gone.

**The sin that was not cruelty**
Now notice carefully what the rich man's sin was, because it is not what we expect, and it is the sin most of us are actually guilty of. He did not have Lazarus beaten. He did not drive him from the gate or curse him or steal from him. There is no act of cruelty in the story at all. His sin was that he walked past. His sin was indifference, the daily, comfortable, unbothered stepping over a name he knew, while he feasted in purple and the man at his gate longed for the scraps. Amos thundered against exactly this, the people who "lie on beds of ivory" and "eat lambs from the flock" and "are not grieved over the ruin" of others (Amos 6:4-6). Not grieved. That is the sin. The law had commanded the opposite: "If among you, one of your brothers should become poor, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but you shall open your hand to him" (Deuteronomy 15:7-8). The rich man hardened his heart and shut his hand and called it living well, and the gate he stepped over became the gulf he could not cross.

And I cannot read this from the side of Lazarus. I have to read it from the side of the man in purple, because by the measure of this world I feast every day, and there are names at my gate I have learned to step over. That is what frightens me about this parable. It does not require me to do anything dramatic to be the rich man. It only requires me to keep walking, to keep my eyes on the table and off the gate, to let the suffering at the edge of my comfortable life become so familiar that I stop seeing it as a person with a name. "If anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?" (1 John 3:17). The judgment in this story falls not on a monster but on a man who simply did not notice, and indifference is a verdict, not an excuse.

The rich man's last request is the most haunting line in it. He begs that Lazarus be sent to warn his five brothers, so they will not come to this place. And Abraham answers, "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them" (Luke 16:29). The rich man protests that if someone rises from the dead, they will repent. And Abraham closes the story with the line that hangs over the whole Gospel: "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead" (Luke 16:31). The heart that will not be moved by the Scripture it already has will not be moved by a resurrection either. Luke knows what we know, that One did rise from the dead, the Son of Man who came to seek the lost, who himself became poor, who had nowhere to lay his head, who took the place of the beggar so that beggars could be carried to Abraham's side. And the warning stands: a hard heart is not softened by miracles. It is softened by the One the Scriptures were always about, or it is not softened at all.

There is still a gate. There is still a name lying at it. And there is still time, which is the one thing the rich man ran out of.

He stepped over a name.

## Up a Tree to See
*Zacchaeus, the Name from the Crowd, and the Thesis of the Whole Gospel*

**Text:** Luke 19:1-10 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 34:11-12 · 1 Timothy 1:15 · 2 Corinthians 5:17 · Galatians 3:7

A small, rich, hated man climbs a tree like a child to catch a glimpse of Jesus passing.

And Jesus stops under the tree, looks up, and says his name.

**Three strikes against him**
Luke gives us Zacchaeus in three quick details, and every one of them is a strike. "He was a chief tax collector and was rich" (Luke 19:2). A chief tax collector, which means he ran a network of tax collectors, which means he grew rich by skimming his own people's taxes for Rome, a collaborator and an extortioner. Rich, by means everyone in Jericho knew were dirty. And "he was small in stature" (Luke 19:3), which is why he cannot see over the crowd, and the crowd has no interest in making room for a man like him. He is despised, he is corrupt, and he is short, and Luke wants us to see all three, because this is precisely the kind of man the religious crowd had given up on. And yet something in him wants to see Jesus badly enough that he abandons all dignity. "So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him" (Luke 19:4). A wealthy, powerful man runs and climbs a tree like a boy. The longing is already at work in him before Jesus says a word.

**The name from below**
Then the moment. "And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today" (Luke 19:5). He says the name. In a crowd that would not make room for the man, would not say his name except as a curse, Jesus looks up into the tree and calls him by name. And then he invites himself to dinner, must stay at your house today, the word must carrying the weight of divine necessity. The Son of God has business at the house of the most hated man in Jericho. The crowd reacts exactly as the grumblers always do. "And when they saw it, they all grumbled, He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner" (Luke 19:7). The same complaint from chapter fifteen, the same offense, that Jesus keeps choosing the wrong houses. The shepherd is doing what the shepherd does. Ezekiel had promised it: "As a shepherd seeks out his flock, so will I seek out my sheep" (Ezekiel 34:11-12). He seeks the one no one else would walk toward.

**The evidence of a changed man**
And the encounter changes the man, visibly, immediately, expensively. Zacchaeus stands and says, "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold" (Luke 19:8). Half his fortune to the poor, and fourfold restitution to everyone he cheated, which was the law's penalty for theft, applied to himself voluntarily. This is not Zacchaeus earning his salvation; this is salvation working itself out through his bank account the same hour it arrived. Grace had reached the one place we are most reluctant to let it reach, the wallet, and the change was real because the encounter was real. "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17). You could see the new creation in the money.

And then Jesus pronounces the verdict over the despised man's house. "Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham" (Luke 19:9). A son of Abraham. The crowd had written him off as a traitor, outside the covenant, beneath the people of God. Jesus restores him to the family, because "it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham" (Galatians 3:7), and the corrupt little tax collector up the tree had more faith in him than the respectable crowd grumbling below.

And here is what I have to face about myself in this scene. I am too often in the crowd, not in the tree. I am the one grumbling about which houses Jesus goes into, deciding in advance who is too far gone, who has done too much damage, who has profited too obviously from sin to be a candidate for grace. The crowd's grumble is my grumble whenever I look at someone and quietly conclude they are the wrong kind of sinner. But the man I have written off is climbing a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus is going to his house tonight, and the only person scandalized by it is me. Paul, who had persecuted the church, called himself the foremost of sinners and the proof of Christ's patience (1 Timothy 1:15). The foremost. The chief. Zacchaeus, chief of tax collectors, foremost of his kind, is exactly who Jesus came for.

And then Luke gives us the line, the one sentence that is the thesis of the entire Gospel, the verse the whole book has been building toward. "For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10). There it is. Not to seek and save the found, the respectable, the religious, the people already inside the crowd. The lost. He came on purpose, traveling toward them, looking up into trees, saying names the crowd spat out, going into houses the crowd would not enter. This is not a Savior who waits at the temple for the worthy to climb to him. This is a shepherd who walks the road to Jericho looking for the one man everybody else had stepped around.

And if that is who he is, then the only question for me is whether I will get down out of the tree of my own making, my hiding, my dignity, my distance, when he calls my name. He knows it. He is looking up.

He came to seek the lost.

## The Table and the Garden
*This Is My Body, and Not My Will*

**Text:** Luke 22:14-23, 39-46 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:5 · Hebrews 5:7-8 · Philippians 2:8 · Jeremiah 31:31-34

In one room he gives his body away as a gift. In a garden a few hours later he begs not to have to.

Both are the same obedience. One is the covenant offered, the other is the covenant paid for.

**The covenant in bread and cup**
At the table, on the night he was betrayed, Jesus does something deliberate with the oldest meal of his people. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says, "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19). Then the cup: "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). The new covenant, the one Jeremiah promised, when God would write his law on hearts and remember sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31-34), is being sealed not in animal blood on an altar but in his own blood, poured out. And he names what the bread means before a nail is driven: given for you. Poured out for you. He is interpreting his own death in advance, telling them that what is about to happen to him is not a tragedy that overtakes him but a gift he is handing over. The body is given. It is not taken.

And then, at that same table, in the same breath of generosity, the shadow. "But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table" (Luke 22:21). The betrayer is eating the bread. Jesus shares the covenant meal with the man who is about to sell him, knowing exactly what he is, and does not throw him out. The grace at that table is wide enough to include the hand that will deliver him to death. That is the kind of love being poured out in the cup.

**The garden where the will breaks**
Then the scene moves to the Mount of Olives, and the man who gave his body so calmly at the table falls to the ground. "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). Hear both halves, because the church is sometimes embarrassed by the first half and should not be. He asks for the cup to pass. He does not want to drink it. The dread is real; this is not a man playing a part, calmly walking through a script. The cost is so great that he prays to be spared it, and Luke, the physician, records the body's response: "And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44). The obedience is not easy and it does not pretend to be. Hebrews tells us he "offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears," and "learned obedience through what he suffered" (Hebrews 5:7-8). The Son of God, sweating blood, learning obedience in the dark.

And the disciples, who should be watching with him, are asleep. He had asked them to pray, and "he found them sleeping for sorrow" (Luke 22:45). The agony is one he carries alone. The cup he must drink, no one can drink with him. The obedience that costs everything is paid in a place where even his closest friends cannot follow him, where they sleep through the worst hour of his life.

**The will that was surrendered for ours**
Here is what the garden shows me about my own heart, and it is not flattering. The whole disaster of the human race began with three words spoken in a garden: not your will. My will. The first Adam, in Eden, said in effect, not your will but mine, and the world broke. And the second Adam, in Gethsemane, in the dark, with the cup of wrath in front of him and his sweat falling like blood, says the exact reverse: "not my will, but yours, be done." Where Adam grasped, Christ surrendered. Where I grasp, every day, in a hundred small refusals to let God's will be done in my life, Christ surrendered totally, in the one place where surrender meant the cross. I pray for the cup to pass and stop there. He prayed for the cup to pass and then drank it. The difference between his obedience and mine is the difference between heaven and hell, and he stood in that gap for me.

Because the cup he did not want to drink was the cup I had filled. It was the wrath my sin deserved, the judgment that should have fallen on me, and he drank it to the bottom so that I would never have to taste it. "He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace" (Isaiah 53:5). The body given for you at the table is the body that would be broken in the morning. The blood poured out in the cup is the blood that would seal the new covenant by paying for every sin it covers. The Son of Man, who came to seek and to save the lost, came knowing it would cost him this, the table and the garden, the gift and the agony, and he set his face to it anyway. "He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:8).

The disciples slept. We would have slept. But he stayed awake, alone, and said yes to the Father's will so that the cup could pass from us forever. And the table he left us is the memory of both halves. Every time the bread is broken and the cup is poured, we are remembering the gift he gave so freely in the upper room and the agony it cost him in the garden a few hours later. The covenant was not cheap. It was offered with calm hands at a table and paid for with bloody sweat on the ground, and the two cannot be separated. The communion meal is not sentiment. It is the body given and the will surrendered, held out to us by the one who did not want to drink the cup and drank it anyway, for us.

Not my will, but yours.

## Paradise for the Last-Minute Thief
*The King Reigning From a Cross, Saving a Guilty Man With Hours to Live*

**Text:** Luke 23:32-49 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:12 · Ephesians 2:8-9 · Colossians 2:15 · Romans 5:6

A man is being executed for his crimes, and he has nothing left, no time, no good deeds, no chance to change.

And he walks into paradise that same afternoon, on the strength of one sentence.

**The prayer over the men with the hammers**
The scene is the worst thing human beings have ever done, and the first words out of the victim's mouth are mercy for the people doing it. "And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left" (Luke 23:33). And then: "And Jesus said, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34). The soldiers are driving nails into his hands, and he is praying for their forgiveness while they do it. This is the love of chapter six made flesh, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, lived out on the cross by the one who commanded it. He prays for the men with the hammers. And around him the mockery comes from every direction, rulers and soldiers and one of the criminals, all saying the same thing in different voices: "He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One" (Luke 23:35). Save yourself. Come down. Prove it. And the terrible irony is that he could not save himself precisely because he was saving them. To save others, he refused to save himself. That refusal is the whole gospel.

**The two thieves and the great divide**
There are two criminals, and they become the great divide of all humanity. One of them joins the mockery: "Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us" (Luke 23:39). Save yourself and us, demanding rescue on his own terms, no repentance, no acknowledgment, just get me down off this. But the other one turns, and in his few remaining minutes he does three things that most religious people never manage in a lifetime. He fears God: "Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?" (Luke 23:40). He confesses his own guilt honestly: "We are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong" (Luke 23:41). And he turns to Jesus with nothing in his hands and asks only to be remembered: "Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom" (Luke 23:42). Think about what this man believes. He is looking at a bleeding, dying, mocked man on a cross next to him, and he calls it a kingdom. He sees a king where everyone else sees a failure. That is faith stripped to its bones, faith with nothing left to add to it, no time to do better, no works to offer, just a guilty man asking a dying king to remember him.

And the answer comes instantly, with no probation, no conditions, no waiting period. "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). Today. Not someday, not after you have proven yourself, not pending review. Today, with me, in paradise. A man whose entire résumé is a criminal record, who has hours to live and not one good deed to bring, is promised paradise on the strength of a single believing sentence. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). No one will ever be saved more purely by grace alone than this thief, because he had no opportunity to add anything to it. He is the proof that salvation is a gift and never a wage.

**The king on the throne of a cross**
And I need this thief, because I keep wanting to bring something. I keep wanting my salvation to have at least a little of my own contribution in it, a record I can point to, a reason I deserved the mercy more than the next person. The thief destroys that. He had nothing. He brought nothing. He got everything. "While we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6). The ungodly. The man on the cross next to him was the ungodly, and so am I, and the only thing either of us could do was ask to be remembered. The good news is not that I can clean myself up enough to deserve a place. The good news is that a guilty man with hours to live got in for free, which means there is room for me.

Because this is a king reigning from a cross. The mockers wanted him to come down to prove his kingship, and they had it exactly backwards: the cross was the throne. Isaiah had said the suffering servant would be "numbered with the transgressors" and would "bear the sin of many" and "make intercession for the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12), and here he is, numbered between two thieves, bearing their sin, interceding for them, doing on Skull Hill the very work the prophet foretold. And in the moment that looked like total defeat, he was actually winning: "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them" (Colossians 2:15). The Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost saves one of them at the last possible second, with his own life draining out, to show that no one is ever too late and no one is ever too far gone.

Then he dies, and a Gentile soldier, a man with no covenant and no temple, looks at how he died and says the truest thing anyone says in the whole chapter: "Certainly this man was innocent" (Luke 23:47), or as the other Gospels render it, the Son of God. The centurion sees it. The thief sees it. The respectable rulers mocking at the foot of the cross do not. Grace finds the criminal and the foreigner, and the religious crowd goes home beating their breasts.

There is room for the worst of us, at the last of all our hours, on the word of a king who saved everyone but himself.

Today, paradise for the last thief.

## The Stranger on the Road
*Burned Hearts, Opened Scriptures, and a Christ Known in the Breaking of Bread*

**Text:** Luke 24:13-35 · **Supporting:** Luke 24:44 · Isaiah 53:3 · 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 · John 5:39

Two men are walking away from the city, away from the empty tomb, away from everything, carrying a hope that has been buried.

And the risen Jesus falls into step beside them, and they do not know him.

**Walking the wrong direction**
This is the third day, the day of the resurrection, and these two disciples are headed in exactly the wrong direction. "That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus" (Luke 24:13), away from Jerusalem, away from the news the women had brought, away from the place where everything was supposedly happening. They are leaving. Their hope is dead, and you leave the place where your hope died. "And Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him" (Luke 24:15-16). He joins them on the road to nowhere, and they do not recognize him, and that is mercy too, because they are not yet ready to see. He asks what they are discussing, and they stop, faces downcast, astonished that this stranger seems to be the only person in Judea who does not know what has happened. And then they tell him, in the saddest tense in the New Testament: "But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel" (Luke 24:21). Had hoped. Past tense.
