The hope is in the grave with the man they followed. They had heard the women's report of an empty tomb and angels, and it had not moved them; it had only confused them. An empty tomb is not enough. You can stand in front of the evidence of the resurrection and still walk the wrong way down the road.

**The Bible study on the road**
Then the stranger does something that is the heart of this whole passage. He does not first reveal himself. He does not perform a miracle to convince them. He opens the Scriptures. "And he said to them, O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?" (Luke 24:25-26). Their problem was not a lack of information about the tomb. Their problem was that they were reading their Bibles wrong, looking for a Messiah who would conquer Rome and never suffer, and so the cross had shattered them instead of saving them. So Jesus gives them the greatest Bible study ever taught. "And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). All of it. The whole Old Testament, from Moses forward, pointed to a Messiah who must suffer and then enter glory. Isaiah had written it plainly, a man "despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3), and they had read past it, the way we read past the parts that do not fit the Savior we wanted. Jesus shows them that the cross was not the failure of the plan. The cross was the plan, written into the text from the beginning. This is what Paul would later call the gospel "of first importance," that "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). In accordance with the Scriptures. It was there the whole time.

**Known at the table**
Then comes the moment, and it is quiet, almost domestic. They reach the village, and the stranger acts as if he would go further, and they urge him to stay, because it is toward evening. And at the table, "he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight" (Luke 24:30-31). He took, blessed, broke, gave, the same four verbs from the upper room, and in the breaking of the bread they finally see him, and then he is gone. And they turn to each other and say the line that names what we all want and rarely get: "Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?" (Luke 24:32). Their hearts had been burning the whole walk, and they had not known why. The risen Christ had been opening the Word, and something in them was responding before their eyes ever did.

And I find myself in these two more than I would like. I have walked the wrong way down the road with a buried hope. I have stood in front of the evidence and felt nothing. I have had Scriptures I knew by heart and somehow missed the Christ they were pointing at the whole time, looking for a Savior who fit my plans instead of the one who suffered and rose. Jesus said it to the religious experts of his day: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me" (John 5:39). You can know the book and miss the One it is about. The resurrection is not a mood you work yourself into, and it is not self-evident from an empty tomb. It is the crucified Christ himself drawing near to slow, grieving hearts, opening the text and then opening the table, until they finally see.

And notice what they do the moment they recognize him. "And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem" (Luke 24:33). That same hour, in the dark, on the road they had just walked in defeat, they run back to the city they had been fleeing. The men walking away from the resurrection become the men running toward the church to announce it. That is what the risen Christ does to a grieving heart, he turns it around on the road and sends it back. The Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost was not finished seeking on Easter morning. He went out after two of them on the road to Emmaus, joined them in their grief, walked with them unrecognized, and opened the Scriptures until their hearts burned and their eyes opened and they could not stay seated.

He is still doing it. He still draws near to slow hearts on the wrong road. He still opens the Word. And he is still known where he has always been known, at the table where the bread is broken.

Slow hearts, the Scriptures opened.
